Q: Avoid wget appending index.html to links A:

I have this same problem.

One thing that might help you with Option 2 is to use

--accept-regex='^http://example.com/website/'

so that you can avoid downloading the entire domain. But you will still need to post-process any files that reference that domain directly.

Q: How to render transparent custom bitmap text in VGA Mode 13h (x86 16-bit Real Mode) without BIOS interrupts? A:

Branchy is fine on a modern CPU for most uses, they're plenty fast especially at this low resolution. You will get branch mispredicts, of course.

x86's only condition stores are the APX version of cmov (in future hardware, nothing has APX yet), or AVX-512 masked stores, or MMX/SSE2 maskmovq/dqu.

The other option would be to load the old data, blend, and unconditionally store, but loads from video RAM aren't fast. Still, could try it with movq xmm1, [es:di], pblendvb xmm1, xmm2 / movq [es:di], xmm0, with the blend mask in XMM0. (https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/pblendvb / is there an inverse instruction to the movemask instruction in intel avx2? / How to efficiently convert an 8-bit bitmap to array of 0/1 integers with x86 SIMD (except that pminub answer produces 0 / 1; use PCMPEQB instead to get 0 / -1 as a control vector for a blend with x & mask == mask).

(To use SSE in real mode, you might need to enable the control-register bits yourself. How do I enable SSE for my freestanding bootable code? . You can't use AVX in real-mode; VEX prefixes conflict with some historical uses of those invalid encodings. Not sure about AVX-512 EVEX prefixes.)

For 8-byte width specifically, MMX maskmovq (https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/maskmovq) might be a good option. Those are NT stores, and are kinda slow on normal (writeback) memory regions, but might be ok on video RAM which is already normally mapped WC (uncacheable write-combining) or even UC (fully uncacheable).

Example using SSE3 pblendvb

  movd   xmm1, ebx
  pxor   xmm4, xmm4    ; XMM4 = 0
  movq   xmm5, [const_bitmask]   ; 0x8040201008040201
  pshufb xmm1, xmm4    ; XMM1 = 8 copies of BL.   SSSE3 instruction

; keep the outer loop over rows
row_loop:
; inner loop over columns of a row replaced with this:
  movd   xmm0, [si]    ; loads 4 bytes, we only care about the first one but that's ok
  pshufb xmm0, xmm4    ; broadcast the font row-bitmap
  pand   xmm0, xmm5    ;   and turn it into a byte-map
  pcmpeqb xmm0, xmm5   ; XMM0 = -1 where x & mask == mask, 0 in other bytes

  movq   xmm3, [es:di]   ; load the old 8 bytes
  pblendvb xmm3, xmm1    ; implicitly uses XMM0 as the blend control.  SSE4 instruction.
  movq   [es:di], xmm3   ; store the 8 updated bytes

 ...
 inc  si
 add  di, 8
 dec  cx
 jnz  row_loop

You could use the same x & mask == mask control-mask with MASKMOVQ instead of with SSE4 PBLENDVB. You'd use MM (MMX) registers instead of XMM (SSE) for that.

(SSSE3 and older instructions have MMX versions, SSE4 and later don't, so I couldn't use MMX registers with a blend unless I wanted to manually blend with PAND / PANDN / POR.) To avoid SSSE3 PSHUFB, you could mov bh, bl / movd mm0, ebx / pshuflw mm0, 0 to broadcast, but partial-register stuff is slower.

If this is in kernel code, you'd need to save / restore the user-space XMM and/or x87 state around code that uses vector registers. e.g. with xsave / xrstor.

Q: How to estimate a QR code redunduncy level? A:

There are some pixels next to the lower left positioning block which indicate the redundancy level. Quote from https://blog.qrstuff.com/2011/12/14/qr-code-error-correction

Quite conveniently, there’s also 2 modules down in the bottom left-hand corner of every QR code that display what the error correction level used in that QR code is.

There is a very nice graphic on that page which visualizes this, which I won't include here as I assume that I'm not licensed to do so.

Q: HAL_Delay() crashes STM A:

As mentioned above, the problem is in HAL_IncTick(). Most likely, you are missing the files: stm32f1xx_it.c and stm32f1xx_it.h.

Download these files from the website STM. Copy:

Core/src/stm32f1xx_it.c, Core/inc/stm32f1xx_it.h

Q: What does the 'b' character do in front of a string literal? A:

it creates a bytes literal, not a normal string.

  • 'the string' is type str (unicode text)
  • b'the string' is type bytes (raw binary data)
b'abc'[0]     # is 97
'abc'[0]      # is 'a'

for concating, you must

'abc' + b'abc'.decode()
# or 
'abc'.encode() + b'abc'

in python2 str was raw bytes, unicode was text

in python3 str is unicode (text), bytes is raw binary data (and b prefix allows explicit creation of byte literals)

there are more:

  • u'' unicode literal
  • r'' raw string
  • f'' f-strings
  • br'' raw bytes
  • fr'' raw f-string
